directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.4405?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect Compared with the law in force on November 18, 2025, the bill adds a duty to publish the Department of Justice’s (DOJ’s) covered Epstein files within 30 days, subject to its listed exceptions: “Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Attorney General shall, subject to subsection (b), make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials in the possession of the Department of Justice” [1].

  • Because Existing public records law allowed some internal government records to be withheld: “inter-agency or intra-agency memorandums or letters that would not be available by law to a party other than an agency in litigation with the agency” [2].
  • Because DOJ had also decided that “no further disclosure would be appropriate or warranted.” [3]
  • Because The bill bars withholding for “embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1].
  • Because It permits withholding portions that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1].

points.title: Public access gives outside investigators another route to pursue overlooked abuse.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Public access gives outside investigators another route to pursue overlooked abuse.

  • Because The bill covers records about “Individuals, including government officials, named or referenced in connection with Epstein's criminal activities” [1].
  • Because Outside scrutiny has already prompted action: “As a result of the Herald's reporting, the top federal prosecutor for the Southern District of New York revived the case and Epstein was arrested in July.” [4]
  • Because Later evidence shows that released federal files can restart an abandoned investigation: “Upon reviewing information recently released by the U.S. Department of Justice, Attorney General Raúl Torrez has ordered that the criminal investigation into allegations of illegal activity at Jeffrey Epstein’s Zorro Ranch be reopened.” [5]
  • So Opening the records lets journalists, witnesses and state investigators check the evidence and press for action when federal handling has left abuse unaddressed. Action against offenders limits their chance to harm more people.
  • Because Sexual violence is a risk in ordinary communities: “It impacts every community and affects both sexes and people of all sexual orientations and ages.” [6]
  • Because Its health harms include “bruising and genital injuries, sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy (for women). Some consequences are psychological, such as depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts.” [6]
  • So Stronger protection against sexual abuse serves [NAME]’s own interest in avoiding injury, infection and lasting mental harm as an ordinary American.
points.con_html:
Response The investigation examples do not show that the added disclosure would stop further abuse by an offender still able to harm people.

  • Because Epstein was already dead before the vote: “On August 10, 2019, Epstein was found hanging in his cell and was later pronounced dead.” [7]
  • Because Maxwell had already received a 20-year prison sentence in June 2022: “to 240 months in prison” [8].
  • Because The Justice Department (DOJ) reported in July 2025: “We did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties.” [3]
  • Because New Mexico’s February 2026 announcement describes its next step as investigating allegations: “revelations outlined in the previously sealed FBI files warrant further examination.” [5] It reports no finding of continuing abuse or offender newly stopped.
  • So The 2019 arrest shows that scrutiny can prompt action, but the person it stopped is dead. The New Mexico announcement supplies evidence of a renewed inquiry, without identifying anyone still able to harm people. The PRO needs that link to connect disclosure to [NAME]’s safety; the health harms of sexual violence do not supply it.

points.title: Opening financial records helps banks and regulators block payments that support sexual exploitation.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Opening financial records helps banks and regulators block payments that support sexual exploitation.

  • Because The bill covers records about “Entities (corporate, nonprofit, academic, or governmental) with known or alleged ties to Epstein's trafficking or financial networks.” [1]
  • Because New York’s banking regulator found that Deutsche Bank missed suspicious payments: “the Bank inexcusably failed to detect or prevent millions of dollars of suspicious transactions.” [9]
  • Because The regulator identified ignored safeguards: “conditions that, if followed, might have detected and prevented many subsequent suspicious transactions” [9].
  • Because Released files have exposed missed bank identity checks. POGO reported that emails showed “six Cerberus guarantors were never identified through the Know Your Client process” [10].
  • Because FinCEN, the Treasury’s financial crime agency, says banks’ information is “vital to identifying human trafficking and stopping the growth of this crime” [11]. It calls for better detection “by becoming aware of the current methodologies that traffickers and facilitators use” [11].
  • So The records give banks payment patterns to check and let regulators examine failures to act. Better checks make it harder to move the money that sustains exploitation. This strengthens a barrier against sexual abuse in the communities where [NAME] lives and works.
points.con_html:
Response The Cerberus example does not connect released files to trafficking payments.

  • Because The Project On Government Oversight describes a failure to check the identities of those backing a financial obligation: “six Cerberus guarantors were never identified through the Know Your Client process” [10]. That passage does not tie those guarantors to trafficking payments.
  • So The Cerberus example supplies no link from its identity-check gap to sexual exploitation. This response does not address the PRO’s separate branches on case records as patterns for banks to check and on regulators examining failures to act.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: New York’s regulator found Deutsche Bank failed to monitor Epstein’s accounts “despite ample information that was publicly available,” and that account conditions “were not transmitted to the majority of the account relationship team.” FinCEN published trafficking red-flag indicators and case studies in 2020, and said “no single red flag is a clear indicator of human trafficking activity.” Sources: [9], [11].

points.title: Opening prosecution decisions helps correct practices that leave abuse poorly investigated.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Opening prosecution decisions helps correct practices that leave abuse poorly investigated.

  • Because The bill covers “Internal DOJ communications, including emails, memos, meeting notes, concerning decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.” [1]
  • Because DOJ’s review found that prosecutor Alexander Acosta ended the federal investigation too soon: “he resolved the federal investigation before significant investigative steps were completed” [7].
  • Because The deal to forgo federal charges was a “unique resolution, and one that required greater oversight and supervision than Acosta provided.” [7]
  • Because DOJ explains how reviewing such conduct helps later cases: “findings resulting from investigations of the conduct of Department attorneys, even former employees, may assist Department managers in supervising future cases.” [7]
  • Because Scrutiny has already changed a practice in this case: “The Palm Beach Sheriff's Office, which had given Epstein work release privileges after his earlier plea to minor charges in state court, discontinued the program.” [4]
  • So The decision records let Congress and the public check where supervision failed and demand tighter review before future abuse cases are closed. Using those findings to improve supervision helps prevent cases from being dropped before the evidence is gathered. [NAME] has a personal safety stake in those safeguards working.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s public 2020 review already examined emails, letters, memoranda and investigative materials and found a need for greater oversight. DOJ guidance effective March 31, 2023 requires best efforts to confer with victims before major case decisions such as non-prosecution agreements. The sheriff’s work-release change occurred by 2019. Sources: [7], [12], [4].

points.title: The records give police lessons for finding and investigating other trafficking operations.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The records give police lessons for finding and investigating other trafficking operations.

  • Because The bill opens records of Epstein’s movements, including “Flight logs or travel records” [1].
  • Because DOJ documented how staff recruited girls: “Epstein used personal assistants to recruit girls to provide massages to him, and in many instances, those massages led to sexual activity.” [7]
  • Because Speaking “As a former FBI Special Agent” [13], Brian Fitzpatrick says full disclosure “is critically important to instruct law enforcement on future human trafficking and exploitation investigations.” [13]
  • So Searchable records let officers outside the original investigation study how recruitment, contacts and travel supported abuse. Those methods give officers patterns to check in other cases, improving the police protection against exploitation that [NAME] shares.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s 2020 review publicly described Epstein’s use of assistants to recruit girls. DHS training on recognizing trafficking existed by 2013. Fitzpatrick’s statement names no specific lesson. Sources: [7], [14], [13].

points.title: The records supply evidence to challenge false trafficking claims used to justify violence against bystanders.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 The records supply evidence to challenge false trafficking claims used to justify violence against bystanders.

  • Because A gunman attacked a pizza restaurant after believing such claims: “Welch was motivated, at least in part, by unfounded rumors concerning a child sex-trafficking ring that supposedly was being perpetrated at the establishment.” [15] “The customers and employees fled the building.” [15]
  • Because Released Epstein files have supplied evidence for corrections. After users claimed that the files proved that theory, Snopes found that “the emails and text messages mentioning "pizza" that many users shared have explanations found elsewhere in the case files.” [16]
  • Because An experiment including Pizzagate tested corrections against seeing false claims alone: “For each fake news example, subjects randomly saw either the fake news story alone, or the story and a correction.” [17]
  • Because Corrections reduced belief in the false stories: “on every issue, corrected subjects on average became significantly less convinced by the fake news story.” [17]
  • So Public records let fact checkers show the context behind false accusations. Evidence-based corrections weaken a false rationale for vigilante attacks. Giving people tools to challenge that rationale serves [NAME]’s interest in staying safe as an ordinary worker or customer in public places.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The correction experiment used 2,742 Mechanical Turk subjects assigned to see a story with or without a correction, and it measured agreement with the story. It did not measure conduct or whether corrections reach people inclined to violence. Snopes reports no measure of its correction’s effect. Sources: [17], [16].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.4405?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on November 18, 2025, the bill would require public release of the Justice Department's unclassified Epstein records within 30 days: “Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act” [1], “make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials” [1]. Its investigation exception covers material that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1].

points.title: Removing lasting protection for confidential sources puts reports that help prevent crime at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing lasting protection for confidential sources puts reports that help prevent crime at risk.

  • Because Existing law allowed the FBI to keep Epstein sources confidential: “The FBI thus properly withheld the names and other identifying information of these sources and the information they provided.” [18]
  • Because The court accepted that breaking promises of secrecy would cause “great detriment to the FBI’s ability to recruit and maintain reliable confidential sources.” [18]
  • Because The bill has no lasting exception for unclassified information identifying sources who are not victims. The House memo warned: “Violating confidentiality would have a chilling effect, deterring future whistleblowers and informants.” [19]
  • Note The victim exception covers “personally identifiable information of victims” [1]. It supplies no lasting protection for a source who is not a victim and whose unclassified information would not jeopardize any active federal case.
  • Because Publication also threatens victims' confidence in reporting. The BBC later documented “botched redactions which revealed the identities of some of Epstein's victims” [20]. It quoted a campaigner's warning: “It creates a sense that if you come forward you will not be protected” [20].
  • Because Help from sources can stop crimes before they harm people. The Justice Department's inspector general quoted the FBI director: “Human sources can mean the difference between the FBI preventing an act of terrorism or crime, or reacting to an incident after the fact.” [21]
  • So Putting source recruitment and safe reporting at risk threatens warnings that police use to prevent harm. [NAME] depends on that protection for personal safety.
points.con_html:
Response Leaving out a separate source exception does not establish that the bill ends source confidentiality.

  • Because The existing Privacy Act bars disclosure of covered personal records, subject to consent and its listed exceptions: “No agency shall disclose any record which is contained in a system of records” [22].
  • Because Courts must preserve laws that can work together: “when two statutes are capable of co-existence, it is the duty of the courts, absent a clearly expressed congressional intention to the contrary, to regard each as effective.” [23] Publishing records with protected identities hidden serves both duties; omission alone does not show that the privacy ban ends.
  • Because DOJ's later protocol applied that existing law to sources. Under “Privacy Act Redactions”, it directs reviewers to hide “Names of confidential sources or cooperating witnesses” [24]. This ground does not depend on victim status or an open investigation.
  • So The PRO has not shown that the mandate requires breaking source promises. This response does not address the PRO’s separate branch on victims’ confidence in reporting after botched redactions.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A June 25, 2026 district-court opinion in Phang v. Blanche granted preliminary relief and explained that the Act requires disclosure beyond ordinary FOIA production. The government did not respond to merits arguments and the court treated them as conceded under its local rule. The passages read do not decide whether the Privacy Act or source-identity protections bind against the Act. This does not settle the open confidentiality question. A September opinion is after the evidence cutoff and excluded. Sources: [25].

points.title: Revealing undercover officers can disable future operations that protect [NAME].
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Revealing undercover officers can disable future operations that protect [NAME].

  • Because Existing law protected the identities of FBI staff in Epstein records, including “FBI special agents and professional personnel” [18].
  • Because The bill has no lasting exception for unclassified undercover identities. The House memo warned: “Release could also publicly reveal the identity of undercover law enforcement officers, preventing them from working in future operations.” [19]
  • Because Later reporting confirms that the files contained such material. CNN reported that “the face of an undercover FBI employee was left uncovered in a video.” [26]
  • Because The Justice Department's guidelines link undercover work to “the detection, prevention, and prosecution of white collar crimes, public corruption, terrorism” [27].
  • Note The active-case rule requires danger to an existing federal investigation or prosecution. It gives no lasting protection for an officer's ability to take future assignments.
  • So Losing an officer's cover weakens future work against dangerous crime. That reduces a means of protection available to ordinary people such as [NAME].
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The one documented undercover exposure was in a 2009 video. DOJ said it failed to obscure the face, and CNN obscured it at DOJ’s request. DOJ’s protocol requires redaction of government employees’ names. The Privacy Act’s definition of a record can include a photograph, and a 2010 appeals ruling applied a law-enforcement privilege to undercover records in discovery. Sources: [26], [24], [22], [28].

points.title: Publishing secret investigative methods gives criminals ways to avoid detection.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Publishing secret investigative methods gives criminals ways to avoid detection.

  • Because Existing law protected methods in the Epstein files. The court upheld the FBI's withholding of “non-public investigative techniques and procedures that it uses to enforce laws.” [18]
  • Because The court accepted a specific danger: “releasing investigative techniques could help criminals evade the law, employ countermeasures, and avoid criminal activities in a particular area to evade detection.” [18]
  • Because The bill's investigation exception requires an “active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution” [1]. It gives no separate protection to unclassified methods that remain useful when no current case would be harmed.
  • So Giving offenders knowledge they can use to escape detection weakens the crime prevention that helps protect [NAME] from harm.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Courts have recognized a qualified law-enforcement privilege that can apply after an investigation ends, and statutes are read with a presumption retaining established principles unless a contrary purpose is evident. No packet source shows that privilege being applied under the Act. DOJ’s protocol lists deliberative-process, work-product and attorney-client privileges. Sources: [29], [28], [30], [24].

points.title: Releasing untested allegations and innocent associations can provoke violence that endangers bystanders.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Releasing untested allegations and innocent associations can provoke violence that endangers bystanders.

  • Because The bill bars withholding to protect reputations: “No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1]. The House memo identified the missing safeguard: “H.R. 4405 requires DOJ to release information, even in cases where DOJ or the FBI has determined it was false.” [19]
  • Because The earlier Epstein ruling recognized physical danger as a reason to protect identities. It accepted the FBI’s view that releasing certain names of people connected with its investigation could lead to “physical harm, or even death.” [18]
  • Because Later reporting shows how publishing research emails can lead to death threats. A professor whose emails were released told Reason: “Some include death threats and many accuse me of being a pedophile who conspired with Epstein to sexually abuse infants.” [31]
  • Because False trafficking stories have already helped cause an armed attack in a public place. DOJ said the Comet Ping Pong attacker acted on “unfounded rumors concerning a child sex-trafficking ring” [15].
  • Because That restaurant was “occupied by employees and customers, including children.” [15] DOJ described the attacker “discharging his assault rifle multiple times into the door.” [15]
  • Because The released files have revived that story. Snopes reported that in February 2026 users alleged that the files “proved the long-debunked "pizzagate" conspiracy theory.” [16]
  • So Publishing names and untested claims supplies targets for threats and risks attacks of a kind that also endangers nearby workers and customers. [NAME] can face that physical danger in those ordinary roles.
points.con_html:
Response The professor’s threats do not show danger reaching ordinary bystanders.

  • Because The professor's reported threats targeted him and his wife over his Epstein correspondence: “My wife and I have received many threatening and malicious emails, texts, and voicemails the past several days” [31]. The evidence identifies targets with a specific Epstein link; it does not show how an added danger reaches unrelated workers or customers.
  • So [NAME]'s ordinary personal safety cannot be inferred from danger to the named contact alone. This response does not address the PRO’s separate route from the revived rumor and the earlier armed attack on a restaurant to risk for nearby workers and customers.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Reason reports that a woman with a sign protested outside Mark Tramo’s workplace, and that no one had accused him of any crime. Snopes concluded the files did not confirm pizzagate. The packet reports no attack on a public place following the release. Sources: [31], [16].

points.title: The required file review takes lawyers away from work that protects people from crime.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 The required file review takes lawyers away from work that protects people from crime.

  • Because The bill requires the release within “30 days after the date of enactment of this Act” [1], making review an immediate duty.
  • Because Bloomberg reported plans to divert 400 Justice Department lawyers to “dedicate all or most of their workdays to complying with the Epstein Files Transparency Act.” [32]
  • Because The review drew on the Criminal Division, whose lawyers were “focused on white collar and violent crime cases” [32].
  • Because National Security Division lawyers had to complete daily review assignments “before they can resume their regular case work” [32].
  • So Review time comes out of time available to investigate threats and prosecute crime. That leaves less staff time for work that protects [NAME]'s personal safety.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Bloomberg reported that lawyers could seek approval to exempt urgent matters, and quoted a statement that attorneys were working “around the clock.” DOJ’s December 2025 letter said most items offices supplied were non-responsive and that a judge’s order added review layers at SDNY. Sources: [32], [33].

  • So Opening the financial-network records gives banks and regulators case details for checking missed warning signs and improving transaction checks.
  • So Stronger checks make it harder to move money that supports trafficking, adding to the country’s defenses against this crime.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: New York’s regulator found Deutsche Bank failed to monitor Epstein’s accounts “despite ample information that was publicly available,” and that account conditions “were not transmitted to the majority of the account relationship team.” FinCEN published trafficking red-flag indicators and case studies in 2020, and said “no single red flag is a clear indicator of human trafficking activity.” Sources: [6], [8].

points.title: Opening prosecution records strengthens checks on decisions to drop serious criminal cases.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Opening prosecution records strengthens checks on decisions to drop serious criminal cases.

  • Because The bill opens “Any immunity deals, non-prosecution agreements, plea bargains, or sealed settlements involving Epstein or his associates.” [1] It also covers internal discussions “concerning decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.” [1]
  • Because The Justice Department’s review found that Acosta’s decision to end the federal case through the agreement “constitutes poor judgment.” [9] It required “greater oversight and supervision than Acosta provided.” [9]
  • Because Public reporting already prompted official scrutiny: DOJ’s inquiry was “in response to a request by Sen. Ben Sasse” [10], “who was critical of the case following a series of stories in the Miami Herald.” [10]
  • So Access to the underlying records lets Congress and the public check prosecutors’ choices and press for stronger review of decisions to end investigations.
  • So Holding those decisions to scrutiny supports a state that can pursue serious crimes even when suspects have powerful lawyers and connections.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s 2020 review included more than 60 interviews and publicly identified a need for greater oversight. DOJ guidelines effective March 31, 2023 address notifying victims of plea and non-prosecution agreements. Sources: [9], [11].

points.title: Opening custody records supports repairs to prison failures that endanger lives and prevent trials.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Opening custody records supports repairs to prison failures that endanger lives and prevent trials.

  • Because The bill opens “Documentation of Epstein's detention or death” [1] and records about “the destruction, deletion, alteration, misplacement, or concealment of documents, recordings, or electronic data related to Epstein” [1].
  • Because DOJ’s prison watchdog found that jail staff made safety checks appear to have happened: “MCC New York staff falsified count slips and round sheets to show that they had been performed when they were not, leaving Epstein unobserved for hours before his death.” [12]
  • Because These failures also blocked a trial. The watchdog found that they “effectively deprived Epstein’s numerous victims of the opportunity to seek justice through the criminal justice process.” [12]
  • Because Missed safety rounds remained a concern in a report issued before the vote. In September 2025, the watchdog reported at another federal detention center: “Correctional Officers did not consistently complete all inmate-monitoring rounds as required by policy” [13].
  • So Outside reviewers gain records for comparing staff logs with witness accounts and identifying failed safety checks. That supports demands for better supervision and reliable records of those checks.
  • So Safer federal custody protects people held by the state and keeps defendants alive for trial, strengthening the state’s ability to protect people and enforce criminal law.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2023 OIG report and its eight recommendations were public. The 2024 Federal Prison Oversight Act requires corrective action plans made public on the inspector general’s site. At SeaTac’s December 2024 inspection, correctional services were staffed at 69 percent. Sources: [12], [14], [13].

points.title: Disclosure gives Congress evidence to check financial ties around defense leadership.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Disclosure gives Congress evidence to check financial ties around defense leadership.

  • Because The bill requires a report to Congress containing “A list of all government officials and politically exposed persons named or referenced in the released materials” [1].
  • Because Feinberg’s defense appointment preceded the vote. A March 2025 report states: “The Senate today confirmed Steve A. Feinberg as the Defense Department's 36th deputy defense secretary” [15]. His duties included “managing the department's budget.” [15]
  • Because Later reporting identifies older emails: “Several emails sent and received by Jeffrey Epstein in 2009 and 2013 suggest that he maintained a business relationship with Cerberus.” [16] Cerberus was “a private equity firm formerly led by Department of Defense Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg.” [16]
  • Because The same report says a tie continues: “Feinberg continues to be financially entangled with Cerberus through a contract for administrative services” [16].
  • So Disclosure gives Congress specific earlier business connections to check against a senior defense official’s duties and ethics disclosures.
  • So Checking for outside financial influence over military decisions and spending helps protect the country’s ability to defend its citizens.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Feinberg’s February 2025 ethics agreement bars participation in certain Cerberus matters while services continue, unless authorized. The Section 3 list covers anyone named or referenced. POGO’s report identifies no specific Defense Department decision affected, and the Pentagon declined to comment. Sources: [17], [1], [16].

points.title: Publicly checkable records give the government a basis for earning trust.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Publicly checkable records give the government a basis for earning trust.

  • Because The bill requires public reasons for blacking out information: “All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress.” [1]
  • Because DOJ’s review found that its handling of information about Epstein’s plea deal “undercut public confidence in the legitimacy of the resulting agreement.” [9]
  • Because The OECD recommends that governments “ensure the data are openly verifiable” [18] as part of earning public trust.
  • Because Trust bears on state stability and effectiveness: “Trust between citizens and their governments is crucial for the legitimacy and functioning of democracies.” [19]
  • So People gain evidence for checking the government’s account and its reasons for leaving details out. This gives public confidence a basis in evidence and officials who must explain their actions, supporting a stable U.S. government.
points.con_html:
Response Making government records checkable does not establish the trust gain on which this stability argument depends.

  • Because A review of experiments involving actual government information states: “The findings of these experiments have been mixed, with effects conditional on the type of respondents and the substantive topic.” [20]
  • Because The OECD’s advice concerns communicating evidence for policy reforms. Alongside verifiable data, it calls on governments to “explain how policy reforms affect the public” [18].
  • So A past loss of confidence from secrecy does not show that publishing this archive would restore confidence. The evidence makes the trust effect depend on the information and its audience. The PRO does not establish the trust gain needed to connect this release to a more stable state.

points.title: Searchable records strengthen factual answers to false trafficking stories that fuel violence.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Searchable records strengthen factual answers to false trafficking stories that fuel violence.

  • Because The bill puts the underlying records in a “searchable and downloadable format” [1].
  • Because False trafficking stories have prompted armed violence. DOJ said the Comet Ping Pong gunman was “motivated, at least in part, by unfounded rumors concerning a child sex-trafficking ring” [21] and described him “discharging his assault rifle multiple times into the door.” [21]
  • Because Released files have already supplied this kind of check. After users claimed that the files proved that theory, Snopes found that “the emails and text messages mentioning "pizza" that many users shared have explanations found elsewhere in the case files.” [22]
  • Because Evidence-based replies can change conspiracy beliefs. A study used AI for “personalized, evidence-based dialogues” [23] and found that “the AI conversations reduced the average participant's belief in their chosen conspiracy theory” [23].
  • So Reporters and public officials gain primary records for checking specific claims and preparing evidence-based replies.
  • So Supplying evidence for those replies strengthens a tool against false stories that have driven armed attacks, serving public safety and social stability.
points.con_html:
Response The dialogue study does not show that the PRO’s proposed replies would change conspiracy beliefs.

  • Because The successful intervention used dialogue, with the AI “adapting its strategy based on each participant’s unique arguments and evidence.” [23] The study measures belief after a personalized conversation; it does not test replies by reporters or officials.
  • So The dialogue study leaves the step from published replies to changed conspiracy belief unsupported. This response does not address the PRO’s branch that released records supply primary material for checking specific claims.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.4405?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill orders DOJ to publish its Epstein- and Maxwell-related files within “30 days after the date of enactment” and to “make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials” [1]. Section 2(c)(1) permits withholding for victims’ privacy, child sexual abuse material, harm to active federal investigations or ongoing prosecutions, images of death, physical abuse, or injury, and properly classified secrets. Its case-protection exception covers material that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1].

points.title: Making secrecy less dependable can reduce the leads and testimony investigators receive.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Making secrecy less dependable can reduce the leads and testimony investigators receive.

  • Because Ordinary federal disclosure law lets DOJ protect confidential sources in law-enforcement records: “could reasonably be expected to disclose the identity of a confidential source” [24].
  • Because The bill has no lasting exception for confidential sources. An analysis entered into the House record warns that release “could publicly identify individuals who were promised confidentiality” [25].
  • Because Breaking those promises discourages future cooperation: “Violating confidentiality would have a chilling effect, deterring future whistleblowers and informants.” [25]
  • Because The mandate also opens the two cases’ grand-jury records, previously protected by the rule keeping that evidence secret. A judicial explanation of the bill’s text states that “Congress overrode Rule 6(e), in the very limited context of the Maxwell and Epstein grand jury materials.” [26]
  • Because The Supreme Court explains why disclosure after a case ends affects future grand-jury witnesses: “Persons called upon to testify will consider the likelihood that their testimony may one day be disclosed to outside parties. Fear of future retribution or social stigma may act as powerful deterrents to those who would come forward and aid the grand jury in the performance of its duties.” [27]
  • Note Temporary protection for a current case cannot preserve secrecy after proceedings end.
  • So Fewer willing sources and less frank testimony leave investigators with less evidence. That weakens the state’s ability to uncover crimes and protect citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO overlooks continuing protection for source identities and does not connect this limited release to less cooperation in other cases.

  • Because Before the bill, the Privacy Act restricted disclosure of covered personal records: “No agency shall disclose any record which is contained in a system of records” [28]. That rule has exceptions; it is separate from the ordinary public-records exemptions the PRO lists.
  • Because DOJ's later instructions applied that existing law alongside the bill. Reviewers were told to hide “Names of confidential sources or cooperating witnesses” [29] under the Privacy Act. This instruction was not limited to active cases.
  • Because The bill separately allows redaction of “personally identifiable information of victims” [1], without an active-case limit.
  • Because The Maxwell grand juries heard no firsthand civilian testimony: “They did not hear testimony from any victim, eyewitness, suspect, or even a records custodian.” [30] This finding concerns those grand juries, not every investigative file.
  • Because The PRO's judicial source reads the bill's reach narrowly: “As to other grand juries, the secrecy of testimony, exhibits, and any other materials remains the rule, subject to the limited exceptions set out in Rule 6(e).” [26]
  • So A general warning about broken promises does not establish that this release would expose protected source identities or make cooperation elsewhere less dependable. The PRO leaves those steps from the bill to reduced cooperation unsupported.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A June 25, 2026 district-court opinion in Phang v. Blanche granted preliminary relief and explained that the Act requires disclosure beyond ordinary FOIA production. The government did not respond to merits arguments and the court treated them as conceded under its local rule. The passages read do not decide whether the Privacy Act or source-identity protections bind against the Act. This does not settle the open confidentiality question. A September opinion is after the evidence cutoff and excluded. Sources: [31].

points.title: Exposing undercover officers can end their use in future operations.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Exposing undercover officers can end their use in future operations.

  • Because Existing disclosure law can protect officers’ names when disclosure threatens their safety. DOJ’s guide says courts use that protection to “protect the identities of law enforcement agents” [32].
  • Because The bill has no separate exception for undercover officers. The House-record analysis warns: “Release could also publicly reveal the identity of undercover law enforcement officers, preventing them from working in future operations.” [25]
  • Because Later reporting confirms such an exposure. CNN reported that “the face of an undercover FBI employee was left uncovered in a video.” [33]
  • Note Temporarily shielding a current investigation does not preserve an officer’s cover for later work.
  • So Losing useful cover weakens the ability to enter criminal groups undetected and stop their crimes. That cuts against [NAME]’s goal of a state able to defend its citizens.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s protocol requires hiding names of government employees including law enforcement, and the Privacy Act’s definition of a record can include a photograph. The documented exposure involved a 2009 video that DOJ called a failure to obscure. Sources: [29], [28], [33].

points.title: Publishing nonpublic police methods and enforcement priorities can help criminals evade the law.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Publishing nonpublic police methods and enforcement priorities can help criminals evade the law.

  • Because Ordinary disclosure law protects information that “would disclose techniques and procedures for law enforcement investigations or prosecutions” [24].
  • Because These files contain such material. A court upheld the FBI’s withholding from Epstein records of “non-public investigative techniques and procedures that it uses to enforce laws.” [34]
  • Because Protected guidelines include rules about which conduct investigators pursue. DOJ’s guide describes the “means by which agencies allocate resources for law enforcement investigations (whether to investigate)” [35].
  • Because The bill has no separate exception for either kind of information. Its mandate expressly includes internal DOJ records “concerning decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.” [1]
  • Because The harm extends beyond the case that produced a record. DOJ’s guide cites a decision protecting surveillance details because disclosure could give wrongdoers insight into FBI capabilities, “possibly jeopardizing similar efforts in the future” [35].
  • Note An exception tied to an active case does not protect a method or enforcement rule merely because it remains useful in later cases.
  • So Revealing how investigators work and when they act helps criminals avoid detection and punishment. That weakens the country’s ability to protect itself against crime.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not connected its forecast about enforcement priorities to a secret rule that the bill newly forces DOJ to reveal.

  • Because The provision about internal records covers “decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates.” [1] Reasons for decisions in particular cases do not by themselves reveal a general rule that criminals can exploit.
  • Because DOJ also applied legal privileges alongside the bill. Its December explanation identifies “deliberative-process privilege, work-product privilege, and attorney-client privilege.” [36] These protect, respectively, internal advice before decisions, lawyers' preparation for cases, and confidential legal advice.
  • So The internal-records provision does not establish that secret instructions or legal strategy must be published. This response does not address the PRO’s separate branch on nonpublic investigative methods.

points.title: Releasing evidence too early can help suspects defeat expected future cases or state investigations.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Releasing evidence too early can help suspects defeat expected future cases or state investigations.

  • Because Ordinary disclosure law can protect a realistically expected enforcement proceeding, not just one already underway. DOJ describes the standard as “pending or reasonably anticipated” [37].
  • Because That protection also reaches state cases: “enforcement proceedings are not limited to federal proceedings or the enforcement of federal law” [38].
  • Because The bill instead names an “active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution” [1]. It gives no separate protection to an expected future case when neither condition applies, or to a state-only investigation before prosecution.
  • Because State-only inquiries do arise in this matter. New Mexico reopened its Zorro Ranch investigation “Upon reviewing information recently released by the U.S. Department of Justice” [39]. That inquiry followed the release, so it shows such inquiries occur, not that the prior rule would have protected this one.
  • Because DOJ’s guide explains that revealing an investigation’s direction can “enable targets to suppress, destroy, or fabricate evidence” [37].
  • So Removing the ground for delaying release in those situations gives suspects a chance to defeat later evidence gathering. That weakens law enforcement’s ability to stop crimes and protect the public.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The FOIA enforcement-proceeding ground requires articulable harm. DOJ and the FBI reported in July 2025 no evidence predicating investigation of uncharged third parties. The Attorney General announced a federal inquiry led by Jay Clayton before the vote, which falls within the bill’s active-investigation exception. New Mexico’s inquiry began after the release, and it reports no lost evidence. New Mexico says its earlier investigation closed in 2019 at the request of the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Because the inquiry was reopened after and because of the release, it does not show a preexisting state case that the prior secrecy rule would have preserved, and it does not show that the release impaired the inquiry. Sources: [37], [40], [41], [39].

points.title: Publishing identifying details can expose people to retaliation.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Publishing identifying details can expose people to retaliation.

  • Because Ordinary disclosure law lets DOJ withhold law-enforcement information whose release “could reasonably be expected to endanger the life or physical safety of any individual” [24].
  • Because The bill protects “personally identifiable information of victims” [1], but lists no general safety exception for nonvictim witnesses, officers, or other people named in the files.
  • Note A witness can remain in danger after the investigation ends, when temporary case protection no longer shields the witness.
  • Because Even permitted victim redactions depend on reviewers finding identifying details before mass publication. A February 2026 filing by victims’ lawyers reports released “Documents containing victims’ names alongside dates of birth, bank information, driver’s license numbers, email addresses, or home addresses.” [42]
  • Because The same filing reports a client saying: “It has been 24 hours and I'm getting death threats whilst nothing is being done.” [42]
  • So The mandate removes a general safety safeguard and makes protection of victims depend on successful review before publication. The resulting exposure to retaliation cuts against [NAME]’s concern for a state that protects its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s separate claim about nonvictims omits the personal-data protections DOJ applied.

  • Because Nonvictims also retain protections beyond the bill's victim exception. DOJ's instructions require redacting source names and “Personal street addresses (street, city, state, zip)” [29] under the existing Privacy Act.
  • So The bill's lack of a general safety exception does not by itself mean that nonvictims’ identifying details are published. This response does not address the PRO's evidence on exposure and threats against victims.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: DOJ told the court on February 2, 2026 that, out of a January 30 upload of more than 3 million pages, it “now has taken down several thousands of documents and media that may have inadvertently included victim-identifying information due to various factors, including technical or human error.” This is an attributed DOJ account, not an independent audit or judicial finding. Several thousand removed items are not several thousand distinct victims or confirmed disclosure events. January 30 was after the 30-day date, so the letter does not establish that the deadline caused the errors, and it does not show the counterfactual extent of disclosure without the Act. Sources: [43].

Evidence note: A June 25, 2026 district-court opinion in Phang v. Blanche granted preliminary relief and explained that the Act requires disclosure beyond ordinary FOIA production. The government did not respond to merits arguments and the court treated them as conceded under its local rule. The passages read do not decide whether the Privacy Act or source-identity protections bind against the Act. This does not settle the open confidentiality question. A September opinion is after the evidence cutoff and excluded. Sources: [31].

points.title: The mass review competes for staff time needed to address other threats.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 The mass review competes for staff time needed to address other threats.

  • Because DOJ’s later compliance report shows the scale of reviewing these files: “More than 500 attorneys and reviewers from the Department” [44] contributed to the effort.
  • Because Reporting on that review describes the “reorienting of resources from both the criminal and national security divisions” [45].
  • So The release duty forces a competing use of staff time needed to investigate and prosecute other threats. That reduces the security work the state can do with those staff hours.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: FBI disclosure review already drew staff in March 2025. DOJ’s count of 500 reviewers does not measure work left undone. Supervisors could approve exemptions for urgent matters. Sources: [46], [44], [47].

points.title: Publishing unchecked accusations supplies fuel for violent conspiracy theories.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Publishing unchecked accusations supplies fuel for violent conspiracy theories.

  • Because The bill bars withholding because of “embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1]. The House-record analysis explains that otherwise releasable information stays subject to disclosure even when false: “H.R. 4405 requires DOJ to release information, even in cases where DOJ or the FBI has determined it was false.” [25]
  • Because Ankush Khardori warns that releasing the raw investigative material would “provide more fodder for more baseless conspiracy theories” [48].
  • Because False trafficking claims have already helped cause an armed attack in the United States. DOJ reports that the Comet Ping Pong attacker “was motivated, at least in part, by unfounded rumors concerning a child sex-trafficking ring that supposedly was being perpetrated at the establishment.” [21]
  • Because DOJ describes what he did: “he carried a loaded AR-15 assault rifle and a revolver into a Northwest Washington pizza restaurant, scattering employees and customers, and fired his assault rifle into a door.” [21]
  • Because The released files have revived that story. Snopes reported that in February 2026 users alleged that the files “proved the long-debunked "pizzagate" conspiracy theory.” [22]
  • So Compulsory publication of unchecked accusations feeds a known route from false trafficking claims to violence. Preventing that danger serves [NAME]’s concern for U.S. safety and stability.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Act also requires release of records on decisions not to investigate or charge. DOJ warned that the production may include fake or falsely submitted material. Snopes concluded the files did not confirm pizzagate. The packet reports no violent act following the release. Sources: [1], [49], [22].

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: H.R.4405 requires the U.S. Attorney General to publicly release all unclassified Department of Justice records about Jeffrey Epstein, including flight logs, names of government officials, and records of his death in custody. It may withhold victims' personal information, active investigations, and properly classified national-security material.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.4405?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If enacted on November 18, 2025, the bill would require the Justice Department (DOJ) to “make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials in the possession of the Department of Justice” [1] concerning the listed Epstein matters, subject to specified exceptions. The deadline is “Not later than 30 days after the date of enactment of this Act” [1]. This adds a broad, timed legal duty to earlier disclosures: a November 18 statement reported that “the Committee has released more than 65,000 pages of records” [2], while DOJ’s July memo had said “no further disclosure would be appropriate or warranted” [3].

points.title: Disclosure carries out the inherited Christian duty to expose wrongdoing.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Disclosure carries out the inherited Christian duty to expose wrongdoing.

  • Because Passing down biblical teaching is an express religious commitment: the Baptist Faith and Message preamble says, “Each generation of Christians bears the responsibility of guarding the treasury of truth that has been entrusted to us” [4].
  • Because The bill bars secrecy merely to spare reputations: “No record shall be withheld, delayed, or redacted on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1].
  • Because Applying Scripture to this case, the Family Research Council’s Washington Stand teaches, “Christians should lead the way in exposing evil to the world and bringing hope and healing to those who are hurting and lost.” [5]
  • So Opening evidence of abuse and its handling puts that inherited rule into practice, including when disclosure embarrasses admired leaders. Following that rule maintains [NAME]’s religious tradition.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A Calvary Chapel writer applying the same duty to Christians’ online posts said “we need to be sure that the evil we're exposing is actually true.” Khardori warned that interview summaries could include uncorroborated derogatory information. DOJ’s FOIA guidance says agencies may not withhold merely on fears of embarrassment. Sources: [6], [7], [8].
points.retirement_reason: Truth and exposing wrongdoing are general moral goals; Christian endorsement does not establish a particular inherited practice affected by disclosure.

points.title: The public record gives families material for passing down Christian sexual morals.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The public record gives families material for passing down Christian sexual morals.

  • Because The release duty covers “Jeffrey Epstein including all investigations, prosecutions, or custodial matters.” [1]
  • Because Focus on the Family’s Daily Citizen connects the case to “the sanctity of marriage and the importance of sexual purity” [9] and says “Christians don’t need to dig too deeply into the offensive drama to use it as a teaching moment, especially for young people” [9].
  • Because The Baptist Faith and Message states, “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [10].
  • So Making the case records public, searchable, and downloadable gives parents who want documented facts evidence to draw on in that teaching. This supports the family practice of handing down biblical sexual morals.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Daily Citizen article, written the day before the vote, says tens of thousands of emails had already been released and that Christians “don’t need to dig too deeply into the offensive drama” to teach from the case. It does not address whether added records would be useful to parents who want documented facts. Sources: [9].

points.title: Disclosure supplies lessons for carrying on Christian work to prevent trafficking and protect children.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Disclosure supplies lessons for carrying on Christian work to prevent trafficking and protect children.

  • Because The bill opens records about entities “with known or alleged ties to Epstein's trafficking or financial networks” [1].
  • Because Former FBI agent Brian Fitzpatrick says disclosure “is critically important to instruct law enforcement on future human trafficking and exploitation investigations” [11].
  • Because Southern Baptists urge believers to “educate themselves and others about the various expressions of modern-day slavery, how to prevent it” [12].
  • Because They also call believers to “stand with our Lord Jesus in loving and protecting children as He does” [13].
  • So The records provide material for the anti-trafficking education this tradition calls for and for training investigators. Supporting those tools puts its duty to protect children into practice.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Southern Baptist Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission pointed churches to trafficking resources in 2020. The Washington Stand already described a recruitment tactic. Fitzpatrick’s statement names no specific lesson. Sources: [14], [5], [11].
points.retirement_reason: Education and training to prevent trafficking serve protection of vulnerable people. A Christian duty to protect children does not establish a distinct traditional practice.

points.title: Scrutiny of officials’ decisions helps uphold the Christian demand for equal civil justice.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Scrutiny of officials’ decisions helps uphold the Christian demand for equal civil justice.

  • Because The bill opens internal DOJ records about “decisions to charge, not charge, investigate, or decline to investigate Epstein or his associates” [1].
  • Because Officials must explain information they hide in released documents: “All redactions must be accompanied by a written justification published in the Federal Register and submitted to Congress.” [1]
  • So The public can examine how officials handled the case and their stated reasons for hiding information in released documents.
  • Because Southern Baptists affirm that “sexual abuse is not only a sin to be disciplined in the context of the church, but also a crime to be prosecuted in the context of civil government” [15].
  • Because The Washington Stand applies that demand to this case: “We cannot allow the other perpetrators to get away with their crimes simply because they are wealthy and privileged.” [5]
  • So Public scrutiny gives [NAME] evidence for pressing officials to apply the law equally to the powerful. That carries the tradition’s demand for civil justice into public life.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ’s OPR publicly found in 2020 that Acosta exercised poor judgment and said: “OPR does not find that it resulted from improper factors.” The redaction-justification rule concerns reasons for hiding information, not findings on charging decisions. Sources: [16], [17], [1].
points.retirement_reason: Equal civil justice belongs to the justice justification in this argument. Calling it Christian duty supplies no substantive additional Tradition connection.

points.title: Giving survivors access to the record supports Christian practices of care and respect for the abused.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Giving survivors access to the record supports Christian practices of care and respect for the abused.

  • Because NPR reports that survivors supported the effort to require DOJ “to release its records in full, with redactions to protect information about victims and ongoing investigations” [18].
  • Because Survivor Marina Lacerda explained the personal need for answers: “They have documents with my name on them that were confiscated from Jeffrey Epstein's house and could help me put the pieces of my own life back together” [18].
  • Because A survivor can recognize her own record after redaction. ABC reported that Maria Farmer, “whose name was redacted from the documents, confirmed to ABC News Friday that she was the complainant.” [19]
  • Because Southern Baptists commend “bringing healing and restoration to trafficking victims in the name of Jesus Christ” [12] and affirm the biblical duty to “honor the dignity and worth of survivors of sexual abuse” [20].
  • So The public-release duty gives survivors access to the releasable records as well as everyone else. Acting on their call for answers puts inherited Christian practices of care and respect into action.
  • Note The bill allows DOJ to withhold the relevant portions of records that “contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy” [1].
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill’s command is to make records publicly available. It creates no separate right for a survivor to inspect information withheld from the public, and victim-related portions may be withheld. Sources: [1].
points.retirement_reason: Respect and care for survivors are the substantive goals; the religious source does not establish a distinct inherited practice affected by disclosure.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.4405?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Judged as of November 18, 2025, the bill would require the Justice Department to “make publicly available in a searchable and downloadable format all unclassified records, documents, communications, and investigative materials” [1] about Epstein and Maxwell within “30 days after the date of enactment of this Act” [1]. Subject to its listed exceptions, it bars withholding for “embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1].

points.title: It removes safeguards against false accusations and rash judgment that inherited Christian teaching rejects.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes safeguards against false accusations and rash judgment that inherited Christian teaching rejects.

  • Because Existing records law permits withholding police records whose release “could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy” [21]. The bill covers people merely “named or referenced in connection with Epstein's criminal activities, civil settlements, immunity or plea agreements, or investigatory proceedings” [1], without requiring a finding of guilt.
  • Because Its mandate reaches rejected accusations. The legal analysis inserted into the House record states: “H.R. 4405 requires DOJ to release information, even in cases where DOJ or the FBI has determined it was false.” [22]
  • Because The Westminster Larger Catechism requires “the preserving and promoting of truth between man and man, and the good name of our neighbor, as well as our own” [23]. The Heidelberg Catechism says not to “join in condemning anyone rashly or without a hearing” [24].
  • Because Rash condemnation has followed the release. Reason reported of a professor whose emails were released that “no one has accused him of any crime whatsoever,” and that “he has been besieged with hate mail, including death threats.” [25]
  • Note True information can also become harmful gossip. Evangelical teaching explains: “But gossip spreads what can include accurate information to diminish another person.” [26]
  • So Publishing false and untested claims in searchable files makes rash judgment and harmful gossip easier. Preserving these inherited duties gives [NAME] a reason to oppose a mandate that denies protection for reputational harm.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Act overrode Rule 6(e) for the Maxwell and Epstein grand-jury materials, but the court had found the Maxwell materials “do not identify any person other than Epstein and Maxwell as having had sexual contact with a minor.” The Act also covers records of decisions not to charge. The Privacy Act requires reasonable efforts at accuracy for some disseminations. Sources: [27], [1], [28].
points.retirement_reason: The objection concerns truthful accusations, reputation and fair treatment. Citing a catechism does not independently establish a Tradition stake.

points.title: It puts survivors' privacy at risk, against Christian ways of caring for people who suffered abuse.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It puts survivors' privacy at risk, against Christian ways of caring for people who suffered abuse.

  • Because Investigators found that “Sensitive information relating to these victims is intertwined throughout the materials.” [3] It includes “physical descriptions, places of birth, associates, and employment history” [3], so removing names alone cannot protect every identity.
  • Because Publishing scattered details lets readers combine them. DOJ's account of the review identifies “the possibility that the media or others in the public will piece together information that in isolation does not identify a victim but can be pieced together to identify a victim” [29].
  • Note The bill permits removing material that contains “personally identifiable information of victims or victims' personal and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy” [1]. That permission does not eliminate the risk from overlooked clues or readers combining details across the required public files.
  • Because Later events show that risk. Victims’ lawyers reported a release “failing to redact victim names and other personally identifying information in thousands of instances” [30]. One client wrote: “I have never come forward! I am now being harassed by the media and others.” [30]
  • Because Christian teaching makes care for survivors a religious practice: “Embracing the victim allows us to emulate God in a tangible way.” [31] The American Association of Christian Counselors makes privacy part of that care: “To share their story without their permission violates trust.” [32]
  • So Making these records public creates a risk of identification survivors did not choose. Maintaining Christian practices of care and confidentiality gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that risk.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The privacy exception covers identifying details and private files, and DOJ’s protocol directs redaction of details that would reveal a victim. The counseling guide concerns a survivor’s personal disclosure to a trusted listener. Sources: [33], [32].

Evidence note: DOJ told the court on February 2, 2026 that, out of a January 30 upload of more than 3 million pages, it “now has taken down several thousands of documents and media that may have inadvertently included victim-identifying information due to various factors, including technical or human error.” This is an attributed DOJ account, not an independent audit or judicial finding. Several thousand removed items are not several thousand distinct victims or confirmed disclosure events. January 30 was after the 30-day date, so the letter does not establish that the deadline caused the errors, and it does not show the counterfactual extent of disclosure without the Act. Sources: [34].
points.retirement_reason: Privacy and confidentiality protect survivors. Describing compassionate care as Christian practice is insufficient without a distinct inherited observance or institution affected.

points.title: It requires public distribution of pornography, undermining traditional Christian sexual rules and religious home life.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It requires public distribution of pornography, undermining traditional Christian sexual rules and religious home life.

  • Because The bill permits withholding material that would “depict or contain child sexual abuse materials (CSAM)” [1], but gives no general exception for adult pornography.
  • Because DOJ's explanation confirms that the mandate reaches sexually explicit videos and images seized from Epstein's devices: the Act “requires public release of these materials” [35].
  • Note Redacting victims does not remove the sexual content. DOJ describes the result as “redacted sexually explicit materials” [35], including videos that appear to be commercial pornography.
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention teaches that “all production, distribution, and consumption of pornographic material is sin against God, neighbor, and self” [36]. It also urges parents to “cultivate homes of holiness” [36] and “protect children from exposure to sexualized media and curb temptation” [36].
  • So The mandate makes the government distribute material this tradition tells Christians to reject. Wider access also adds to the sexual material parents must guard against. Preserving these sexual rules and ways of raising children gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that distribution.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: DOJ says females in the videos and images were redacted, and anyone entering its Epstein library must verify they are over 18. The DOJ letter does not describe what imagery remained visible. Sources: [35].

points.title: It puts lawful promises of secrecy and the safety of confidential sources at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It puts lawful promises of secrecy and the safety of confidential sources at risk.

  • Because Existing records law protects information whose release “could reasonably be expected to disclose the identity of a confidential source” [21]. It also protects against release that “could reasonably be expected to endanger the life or physical safety of any individual” [21].
  • Because These are real interests in the Epstein files. A 2022 court decision found: “The FBI therefore offers probative evidence that these sources received express assurances of confidentiality.” [37] It also found that disclosure of confidential-source information “could subject the sources to reprisal” [37].
  • Because The bill carries over no separate exception for confidential sources or their safety. Its police-work exception concerns material that “would jeopardize an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution, provided that such withholding is narrowly tailored and temporary” [1]. A promise of secrecy is not itself one of its grounds for withholding.
  • Because The Westminster Larger Catechism requires “keeping of lawful promises” [23]. Its teaching on preserving life also requires “protecting and defending the innocent” [38].
  • So Requiring disclosure without these standing safeguards puts sources' trust and safety at risk even after a case ends. Keeping inherited Christian duties to honor lawful promises and protect innocent people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that loss.
points.con_html:
Response Omitting public-records exemptions does not by itself end other source protections or turn legally qualified assurances into broken promises.

  • Because A separate court-made rule protects informants’ safety. In a case about required disclosure of wiretap applications, a federal appeals court held: “Statutes requiring disclosure, but silent on the question of privilege, do not override customary privileges.” [39] It upheld withholding details that would expose an informant.
  • Because H.R.4405 does not expressly end that rule. Its express ban concerns “embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity” [1]; that is not a ban on protection against physical reprisals. Listing omitted public-records exemptions does not resolve the separate rule.
  • Because DOJ’s later protocol lists “Names of confidential sources or cooperating witnesses” [33] among redactions it requires.
  • Because The FBI’s preexisting instructions require telling sources that the government “will strive to protect the Confidential Human Source's identity but cannot guarantee that it will not be divulged” [40]. They require disclosure “when required by court order, law, regulation” [40].
  • So The PRO has not established that the bill forces exposure despite independent source protections. Disclosure reserved by the terms of an assurance also does not establish a breach of the Christian duty to keep lawful promises.
points.retirement_reason: Confidential promises and source safety concern integrity and protection; the religious label adds no distinct Tradition justification.

points.title: It exposes police methods needed for future cases, against the traditional Christian duty of government to restrain wrongdoing.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It exposes police methods needed for future cases, against the traditional Christian duty of government to restrain wrongdoing.

  • Because Existing records law protects information that “would disclose techniques and procedures for law enforcement investigations or prosecutions” [21]. That protection is not limited to an active case.
  • Because The Epstein records contain such methods. The 2022 court decision found that the FBI had protected “non-public investigative techniques and procedures that it uses to enforce laws” [37]. It accepted a specific danger: “releasing investigative techniques could help criminals evade the law, employ countermeasures, and avoid criminal activities in a particular area to evade detection” [37].
  • Because The bill gives no general exception for unclassified police methods needed in future cases. Its exception instead covers harm to “an active federal investigation or ongoing prosecution” [1].
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention states: “Civil government is ordained by God to restrain evil and to promote that which is good” [36].
  • So Compelling disclosure of reusable methods outside the bill's exceptions puts future investigations at risk. Preserving the government's ability to carry out this inherited Christian role gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that exposure.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A qualified law-enforcement privilege can apply after an investigation ends, and one appeals court said disclosure statutes silent on privilege do not override customary privileges. No packet source shows it being applied under the Act. The bill’s active-federal-investigation exception covers any active federal case. Sources: [41], [39], [1].
points.retirement_reason: Preserving investigative capacity concerns public security. Religious endorsement of the state's protective role is not an affected inherited practice.

points.title: It threatens the political support needed to sustain traditional Christian practices in public life.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It threatens the political support needed to sustain traditional Christian practices in public life.

  • Because Alongside its ban on withholding for political sensitivity, the bill requires “A list of all government officials and politically exposed persons named or referenced in the released materials” [1].
  • Because Earlier disclosures show a risk to Trump and his coalition. Reuters described newly released emails as “a potential vulnerability for Trump that could shadow the president and his Republican Party into next year's midterm congressional elections” [42]. It also reported that the controversy “complicates his effort to keep his coalition focused on policy rather than scandal” [42].
  • Because Legal commentary on this bill connects further publication to further controversy. Releasing the raw files would “provide more fodder for more baseless conspiracy theories, potentially for years to come and with no end in sight” [7].
  • Because Trump's administration advances specific religious and cultural practices. Associated Press reported: “His administration and his Supreme Court appointees have expanded areas for religious exemptions and expression in the public square.” [43] It also reported an order “recognizing only male and female as biologically determined sexes” [43].
  • So Further mandatory disclosures create a political risk for the coalition advancing religious expression and the religious right's view of sex. Preserving its ability to sustain those practices gives [NAME] an additional reason grounded in Tradition to oppose the mandate.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect mandatory disclosure to an added risk to the coalition’s ability to sustain Christian practices.

  • Because Reuters quotes a strategist’s forecast that the controversy “could depress Republican turnout in the 2026 midterm elections if new revelations keep dripping out” [42]. That condition concerns continued piecemeal revelations; the bill requires disclosure within “30 days after the date of enactment of this Act” [1]. The PRO does not establish that these produce the same political risk.
  • Because Reuters also identifies a different cause of prolonged attention: “The continued attempts by the White House to suppress or deflect news around the saga have had the effect of prolonging the attention paid to it, they said.” [42] The quoted vulnerability cannot simply be attributed to disclosure rather than the handling of disclosure.
  • Because On November 18, Family Research Council president Tony Perkins identified the problem as “the perception of a cover-up” [44] and argued that “the only way to prevent this political storm from becoming a political disaster is transparency” [44].
  • Because The PRO’s legal commentator predicts that disclosure would “provide more fodder for more baseless conspiracy theories” [7]. That predicts more speculation, without establishing its effect on the coalition’s ability to sustain religious practices.
  • So The PRO combines a forecast about continued piecemeal revelations with a prediction of more speculation. Those claims do not establish that this disclosure mandate adds the threat to Christian practices on which its Tradition argument depends.
points.retirement_reason: The chain runs through political damage to a favored coalition. It does not substantiate the further claim that a particular religious practice or transmission would be impaired.
